## gazefov v0.1.0 — IR eye tracking + foveated Gaussian-splat rendering

### Highlights
- Ray-traced synthetic IR eye camera with exact ground truth (refracting cornea, lids, lashes,
  8-LED glints, noise/blur/occluders, headset slippage).
- Hand-written pupil + glint pipeline (threshold sweep, morphology, Starburst, RANSAC ellipse,
  RANSAC glint-to-LED association) and two gaze estimators with 9-point per-user calibration.
- 🧪 Synthetic benchmark (8 subjects, 2 560 held-out frames): calibrated 3D model 0.08° median /
  0.38° p95 at low noise and 0.12° median at 3 mm slippage, where PCCR + polynomial reaches 4.56°.
- Foveated splat renderer for WebGPU (splatweb v0.1.0 core, shared preprocess + sort, low-res
  periphery + full-res inset, smooth blend). Measured on an RTX 2060 via Dawn at 2160×2160: up to
  ~30 % lower GPU frame time with a 5° fovea and a 1/3–1/4 periphery (interleaved A/B timing), fovea
  PSNR ≥ 70 dB vs full resolution; larger foveae (≥ 15°) are slower than full resolution — see the
  README for the full table and why.
- GZFV 92-byte UDP gaze packet (Python + TypeScript), UDP→WebSocket relay, 1€ filter, Vanta adapter
  interface, IEC 62471 LED exposure budget, camera hooks.

### Downloads
- `gazefov-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl`, `gazefov-0.1.0.tar.gz` — the Python tracker.
- `gazefov-render-0.1.0.tgz` — the renderer sources (npm pack), `gazefov-render-demo.tar.gz` — built
  browser demo (needs a WebGPU browser).
- `gaze_accuracy.md`, `foveation_bench.json` — the measured results behind the README.

### Not yet verified
- No real headset, IR camera or LED ring: hardware notes, eye-safety and latency numbers are
  calculations from stated assumptions.
- No real IR eye dataset evaluated; all gaze accuracy is synthetic.
- The numpy tracker is a reference implementation (≈ 158 ms/frame here), not real-time.
- The Vanta adapter is an interface + host-agnostic driver; mapping it to Vanta needs Vanta's API.
- GPU timings were taken on a GPU shared with other jobs; absolute milliseconds are noisy.
